claim: In rule-based matrix and series items, difficulty rises steeply with the number of simultaneous rules or sub-goals to hold (Raven error about 16% at one rule token vs about 59% at three or four; rule tokens explain 57% of item error variance in the founding study). Rule count is a real but partial predictor. Gap search: the 57% and r=.87 were confirmed in the 1990 text but rest on 12 students and 32 items; no larger-sample replication was found.
agent_test: On ARC-like or puzzle items, count rules/sub-goals with a code-side counter, then check rank correlation with the agent's pass rate at equal tokens; compare against a length-only baseline.
audit_note: Minor: the 57%/45%/32 problems figures were confirmed from the original abstract; the Table 3 averages (16% vs 59%) and 12 students could not be re-read directly (publisher pages blocked); a01 and d15 are the same paper.

claim: Rule count and type are not enough: generated-matrix sets explain difficulty only partly (23-item set, 307 participants: 'far from enough'; early banks about 40% of variance), and distractors and perceptual features need their own terms. Gap search: Embretson and Daniel 2008 (101 GRE items, 534 students) give R2 .451 and .435 in-sample, so about half of difficulty is explained by cognitive features on real items.
agent_test: Add distractor-count and perceptual-complexity slots to the S0 feature list and measure the gain in rank correlation over rule count alone.

claim: Text-based difficulty prediction across 37 studies is moderate: Pearson r mean .545 (range .04-.87, N=17), R2 mean .478 (N=13). Best published values are ceilings. Single studies agree (Kapoor r .77, Razavi within-grade r .37-.70).
agent_test: Pre-register that the S0 estimator is expected to reach rank rho about .5, not .8, and report both rank and error metrics.
audit_note: Minor: Razavi .37-.70 is the by-grade range of the feature-based model (not direct estimates); a11 and b01 are the same review.

claim: Direct judgments of difficulty (by experts or by an LLM asked for a number or label) are weak: experts r as low as .38 vs IRT; LLMs rho .31-.37 on ENEM, below .50 average over 20 models, near zero on NAEP math (-0.14 to 0.14) and on LLM-labelled course questions (rho .06).
agent_test: Compare the agent asking itself 'how hard is this?' against a counted feature or a 3-sample pass rate at equal tokens; expect the self-rating to lose.
audit_note: Minor: ENEM best-prompt rho spans about 0.10-0.37 across ten models, so '.31-.37' describes only the top models; page summary of Brant et al. gave conflicting per-model values (o3 .31 vs .37) and Li et al. table-average is 0.28 over 21 models.

claim: Better design: have the LLM fill named feature slots (steps, cognitive load, misconceptions) and let code regress, rather than ask for one number. Gains: math RMSE 0.83 vs 0.91 direct, r .87 vs .83 (Razavi); holdout Pearson .78 with LLM features vs .68 embeddings alone (Hoyl). Caveat: the Razavi gains are pooled across grades.
agent_test: S0 variant A: model outputs one difficulty number. Variant B: model fills 6 feature slots, code maps to a bin. Same tokens; compare agreement with measured pass rate within a task family.
audit_note: Minor: Hoyl's target is real student correctness, with simulated responses as output, and the .78 vs .68 is the embedding-only ablation; a13/b03/c03/c04 are the same Razavi paper.

claim: Pooled correlations across levels (grades) overstate skill; within a level, prediction is much weaker and can be no better than a level-mean baseline (grade K math RMSE worse than dummy; grade 1 math R2 .003; within-grade feature r .37-.70).
agent_test: Evaluate any S0 gate inside one task family and against a family-mean baseline, never on a pooled easy-plus-hard set.

claim: Aggregating many simulated attempts gives usable difficulty only under conditions: NAEP simulated classrooms reach r up to .75/.76/.82 (grades 4/8/12), but zero-shot unaligned simulation is weak (SMART PCC .265 vs .649 aligned) and persona effects are unstable in another study. Weaker models can simulate better than stronger ones.
agent_test: Run 5, 10, 20 cheap samples per item with varied prompts and measure how pass-rate rank agreement grows with samples; check that samples come from varied prompts, not one persona.

claim: LLM uncertainty (first-token probability, choice-order sensitivity) is a real but small difficulty cue: adding it to text features cut test RMSE by about 0.02-0.03 relative to a mean-predicting dummy (Biopsychology .1361 vs .1667; USMLE .2868 vs .3110) but only about 0.01 relative to text-only TF-IDF on Biopsychology (.1479 to .1361); correlation with student answer distributions is weak and differs for right vs wrong answers. A hidden-state probe reaches ROC-AUC 93.09% on ScienceQA for the model's own failures (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) but needs white-box access.
agent_test: Use sample disagreement or answer-token confidence from the first pass as an S0 feature; test if adding it to a feature count lifts rank rho at equal tokens. Split results by whether the answer passed a check.
audit_note: The 0.02-0.03 RMSE gains quoted (.1361 vs .1667, .2868 vs .3110) are against the dummy baseline, not text features; over text-only TF-IDF the Biopsychology gain is about 0.012 (.1479 to .1361).
claim_before_audit: LLM uncertainty (first-token probability, choice-order sensitivity) is a real but small difficulty cue: about 0.02-0.03 RMSE gain over text features (Biopsychology .1361 vs .1667 dummy; USMLE .2868 vs .3110), and weak correlation with student answer distributions that differs for right vs wrong answers. A hidden-state probe reaches ROC-AUC 93.09% on ScienceQA for the model's own failures but needs white-box access.

claim: Stronger models call more items easy and compress their estimates: GPT-5 predicted easy for 56.9% of hard items and 89.3% of medium items (and none as hard), GPT-4.1 was best at 3-level QWK .578; bigger or reasoning models are not better aligned with humans (GPT-5 rho .34 vs GPT-4.1 .44); ENEM estimates too easy; reading near-ceiling models compress IRT spread.
agent_test: Track the agent's predicted-easy share against measured pass rate as the base model gets stronger; recalibrate the S0 threshold per model.
audit_note: Minor: the evidence line mislabels the GPT-5 table as hit rates; the confusion table shows GPT-5 predicting easy for 89.3% of medium and 56.9% of hard items and never hard, which matches the claim.

claim: Difficulty for humans and for models are different quantities: items hard for humans are often trivial for models (Savant rate 70.4% USMLE, 32.2% SAT Math), open multimodal LLMs sit near chance on matrices people solve at 95.9%, and ARC-AGI-2 difficulty is defined by human pass rate. S0 must measure difficulty for the solver in use. Gap search: probes show human IRT difficulty and a model's own difficulty correlate 0.65 falling to 0.45 as reasoning level rises (GPT-OSS-20B).
agent_test: Compute rank correlation between a human-based difficulty index (ARC human pass rate) and the agent's own pass rate; use the agent's own pass rate to route.
audit_note: Minor: 0.65 to 0.45 is an approximate figure read from a plot and is between human IRT and the probe-predicted (not empirical) model difficulty; the open multimodal models are near chance on 3 matrix sets, humans 95.9% was on IQ50 only.

claim: The best test-time search method depends on problem difficulty, and difficulty should be defined by absolute pass rate (easy 50-100%, medium 10-50%, hard 0-10% Pass@1), not by quantile bins, because Qwen2.5-72B has Pass@1 above 80% on 76.2% of MATH-500. Estimated difficulty also lets Self-Consistency, Best-of-N and Self-Refine use fewer tokens at similar accuracy.
agent_test: Route items to shallow, best-of-N or tree search by a 3-5 sample pass-rate gate with absolute thresholds, and compare against fixed-depth search at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Zhu et al. abstract states fewer generated tokens but does not state accuracy stays similar; at 72B Liu et al. find best-of-N best at every level, so 'depends on difficulty' holds for smaller models.

claim: A model's own labels of Easy/Medium/Hard on its own questions track formatting, not difficulty (label vs empirical rho .06; label vs Bloom level .90). GPT-4 pairwise judgments match humans on large gaps but rank poorly against IRT (Spearman .612 GSM8K, .218 ARC, .164 Winogrande).
agent_test: Block any use of the model's self-assigned difficulty label as a routing input; allow it only as a coarse easy-versus-hard gate and log its error.
audit_note: Minor: Easy2Hard-Bench main text gives GPT-4 vs human matching 0.84/0.62/0.60 while the appendix table has 0.922/0.825/0.771; the Spearman values .612/.218/.164 match the table; the claim's 'match humans on large gaps' is the weaker point.

claim: For ranking which of two items is harder, pairwise comparison beats absolute rating in most configurations; token probabilities plus labelled examples lift absolute rating to a similar level.
agent_test: When the agent must order sub-problems, compare pairwise comparisons counted in code with absolute scores, same token budget, and check agreement with measured pass rate.

claim: One cheap feature family carries most of the text signal: in Kapoor et al. linguistic features alone (r about .75, RMSE .62) and ModernBERT embeddings alone (r .76, RMSE .62) nearly match all features (r .76-.77, RMSE .59); TF-IDF adds nothing over a dummy for math (Razavi, RMSE 1.01 both); basic question features add almost nothing once embeddings exist (Hoyl, .6822 to .6842). A small engineered feature set can beat 768-dimensional BERT embeddings (RMSE .302 vs .614 in Fulari and Rusert, cited by Peters et al., which attribute it to dimensionality).
agent_test: Compare a 5-feature count against a longer feature stack on a held-out set of our own items; stop adding estimators when rank rho stops moving.
audit_note: Peters et al. attribute the Fulari and Rusert result (RMSE .302 vs .614) to the curse of dimensionality, not to little data; also Kapoor's linguistic-only row reads r .75 / RMSE .62 in the fetched version, not .76.
claim_before_audit: One cheap feature family carries most of the text signal: linguistic features alone give r .76 and LLM embeddings alone r .76, all features r .77 (Kapoor); TF-IDF adds nothing over a dummy for math (Razavi); basic text features add nothing once embeddings exist (Hoyl). Small hand-picked feature sets can beat large embeddings with little data (RMSE .302 vs .614 in one study).

claim: A feature-only difficulty estimate is a prior, not a measurement: in adaptive-test simulation LLTM needs explained variance of about 75% or more to match calibrated Rasch precision at RMSE 0.4, and extra items needed fall as R2 rises. Typical text models (R2 about .48) fall below that.
agent_test: Treat the S0 estimate as a prior and update it with observed check outcomes after the first attempt; measure whether the update beats the prior alone.

claim: A first solve attempt's process cost carries difficulty information: mean correct response time correlated r=.87 with Raven error rate across items; reasoning-trace episode features add an 8.1% relative gain over fine-tuned baselines in human difficulty classification; propagated model-failure counts reach 90% agreement with human difficulty. Gap search: on H-ARC, reasoning-trace length correlates only 0.16-0.30 with human item time, and within an item failed attempts are longer than successes.
agent_test: Log tokens used and number of revision loops in a first attempt; test whether they predict final failure beyond a feature count at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the .87 Raven time-error correlation was only confirmed through a secondary text extraction of the paper; RankLLM's 90% is agreement with human judgments (not strictly difficulty labels); epi2diff gain is over supervised LLM fine-tuning on SAT-derived tasks.

claim: Report rank correlation and error together: a mean predictor attains the lowest RMSE (1.19 on ENEM) with rho 0, and formats such as RMSE (31.8% of metric uses) differ across studies, blocking comparison.
agent_test: For every S0 test, report Spearman rho plus RMSE against a mean-predictor baseline.
audit_note: Minor: Brant et al. per-model best rho and metric counts consistent with Peters et al. (RMSE in 31.82% of metric uses, 28 uses).

claim: Averaging correlated raters adds little and can dilute: three professors averaged did no better than single raters; the model ensemble on SAT Math rose from rho .56 to a peak of .66, then declined past K=14 models, and fell at once on USMLE.
agent_test: Compare k=1,3,5 samples from one model with k samples from different prompts or models on the S0 estimate; stop adding when gain ends.
audit_note: Minor: Li et al. show SAT Math ensembling first improved correlation (0.56 to 0.66), so 'adds little' applies mainly to the professors and to USMLE (dilution immediately); 'correlated raters' is the claim's interpretation.

claim: A probe or estimator trained in one domain loses accuracy in another, and each target model needs its own (hidden-state probe; BEA USMLE tasks barely beat a dummy: RMSE .29 vs .31). Calibrate per task family. Gap search: a coding-agent difficulty model trained on three benchmarks reaches AUC .67-.74 on a fourth (base rate .57-.64, oracle .91); a math probe loses accuracy across datasets.
agent_test: Fit S0 on one task family, test on another, and report the drop; require re-calibration whenever the family changes.
audit_note: Minor: Zhu et al. also say the method 'maintains strong performance under domain shifts' (ScienceQA to MMBench 89.03) with a weak StrategyQA to CommonsenseQA transfer (65.69) and cross-model transfer ~47-50; Ge et al. .571/.637 are baseline AUCs, not base rates, and the .67-.74 range is the feature models.

claim: No 2020-2026 paper found that runs Embretson-style cognitive design (stimulus features to difficulty to adaptation) inside an LLM agent loop. Gap search found IRT used for model routing (IRT-Router, +3% over GPT-4o alone at 1/30 cost) and IRT with task features for predicting agent success on coding benchmarks (AUC .83-.84 on new tasks), and many allocation methods that use pass rate or sampling disagreement instead of IRT. Absence is under a limited search (web quota ran out twice).
agent_test: Second search sweep (see GAPS); if still empty, treat the S0 gate result on our agent as new evidence.

claim: A pre-solve difficulty signal improves accuracy at equal budget, but gains are modest and conditional: sampling-disagreement allocation +2.3 points average (up to +5.5), at N=16 no significant gain; a 16-feature text classifier +4 to +6 points on MATH within about 1 point of the oracle allocation; hidden-state predictor +7.9 on GSM8K. All use math sets and the last two need training data from the same family.
agent_test: Run S0-gated depth vs fixed depth at equal total tokens (probe included) on a held-out task family; report accuracy per 1k tokens.
audit_note: Minor: UAB's five benchmarks include MMLU Formal Logic (not math), and at N=16 two Qwen2.5-7B settings significantly favor uniform; AdaCompute +4 to +6 is 4.5-6.4 points on MATH with oracle gap about 0.9-1.4.

claim: A sampling probe can cost more than it saves: with k=10 samples on a 12x model-size pair, routing costs 1.38x always-large even at AUROC .871; at k=5 it dominates (cost 9.8-11.6 vs 12.0, accuracy .508-.520 vs .484). Break-even needs a cost ratio above 11.1 at k=10 and a 10% escalation rate.
agent_test: Count probe tokens in the budget; test k=2,3,5 and stop at the smallest k that keeps the rank signal.

claim: Few samples suffice to rank difficulty for the model itself: two samples (vote entropy) gave AUROC .780 vs phase-1 correctness and beat an annotated-difficulty oracle in allocation quality; five samples matched ten (T2 AUROC .865 vs .862) while three lost about .07. Hardest items gain least because the right answer is not sampled.
agent_test: Use 2 to 5 probe samples; flag items where all probe answers disagree as 'maybe unreachable' rather than giving them more of the same sampling.
audit_note: Minor: the beat-the-oracle comparison holds only on MATH500 and Graded Arithmetic (the sets where the annotated-difficulty oracle exists); the k=3/5/10 AUROC figures come from a different paper (Pishehvar et al., semantic entropy for routing on Gemma-3) than the .780 figure (UAB), so the combined sentence merges two setups.

claim: There is no published per-task correlation between human pass rate and model pass rate on ARC-AGI-2; ARC-AGI-2 model scores of 1-3% at release left no variance to test. The human side is documented (407 participants, 13,405 attempts, 62% solved). On ARC-AGI-1, grid size predicts human difficulty weakly (r -0.16 training, -0.02 evaluation) and reasoning-trace length correlates .16-.30 with human item time.
agent_test: Fit rule-count and grid-size features to the agent's own pass rate on ARC tasks; do not assume human pass rate is the target.

claim: Inside one item, a longer reasoning trace is a failure sign for models (wrong-minus-right d>0 for all five thinking models) while the opposite holds for humans (d=-0.10); the pooled item-controlled interaction is -0.66 log units. A symbolic ARC solver's mid-run grid state predicts success at held-out AUC .765 and supports early stopping that saves 33.6% of compute at 98.9% solve rate kept.
agent_test: In S3-S5, log tokens spent per attempt; test a rule 'escalate or restart when a trace exceeds the item's first-attempt median' against fixed budgets.
audit_note: Minor: Pendharkar notes reallocating the saved compute did not raise solve counts and the held-out AUC rests on 41 entries from 38 tasks; per-model d values appear only in a figure (text range 1.47-3.13, with two models descriptive).

claim: Always score a free question-only difficulty estimate next to any model-based signal: on synthetic arithmetic a regex difficulty score matched semantic entropy (AUROC .839/.830 vs .830/.867) and on GSM8K entropy beat it by .21-.31. A result that does not beat the free baseline adds nothing.
agent_test: Include a text-only difficulty baseline arm in every S0 test.

claim: API-only agents can read the reliability of a finished answer from fixed follow-up questions (AUROC .73-.79 on GSM8K and CodeContests for GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5) while verbal confidence sits near chance (.42-.55). This predicts correctness of a finished answer, not the difficulty of a new problem, and needs a trained predictor per model.
agent_test: Test a small bank of follow-up questions after the first answer as a reliability check before committing, trained on past runs.
